background.definition: Achilles pain is caused by three distinct entities: Achilles tendinopathy, Achilles enthesopathy, and bursitis. Tendinopathy is a clinical term for midsubstance tendon degeneration. Enthesopathy refers to degeneration of the tendon at its insertion into the bone. Bursitis occurring in the Achilles region typically involves the retrocalcaneal bursa or the adventitial bursa between the Achilles and the skin. Achilles tendinosis is a chronic, non-inflammatory, degenerative process of the middle third of the tendon and typically presents as a painful, tender nodule 3 to 4cm above the calcaneal insertion. Achilles enthesopathy results from non-inflammatory degradation of the Achilles insertion at the calcaneus. Retrocalcaneal bursitis and adventitial bursitis are true inflammatory processes, typically caused by excessive compression from ill-fitting footwear. Haglund's deformity is a calcaneal ostosis that when present can prolong and complicate the treatment of all Achilles pain disorders.

Achilles tendinopathy accounts for 66% of Achilles injuries, making it the most common injury in the Achilles region.
Achilles enthesopathy is the second most common Achilles injury.
Overuse such as increased mileage and hill running can cause Achilles tendinopathy.
Overuse, tight fitting shoes and Haglund's deformity predispose to Achilles enthesopathy and bursitis.
Males are more likely to have Achilles pain than females.
A history of previous Achilles injury predisposes to future Achilles pain.
Achilles pain may be seen as a complication of fluoroquinolone use, especially in the elderly.

Achilles tendinopathy is characterized by collagen degeneration, altered ground substance deposition, and a complete lack of inflammatory cells. These histologic features define tendinosis. Neovascularization, increased proteoglycan production and formation of disorganized immature collagen are also prominent features of chronic tendinosis. Recent studies suggest that tendon neovascularization may be the pain generator in Achilles tendinopathy.
The histology of Achilles enthesopathy is less well described.
In retrocalcaneal and adventitial bursitis, compression of the bursa results in swelling and a classic inflammatory reaction.
Gait-related risk factors could be considered, but it is not known whether addressing these would prevent injury.

There are no data on stretching, bracing, strengthening or footwear modification in prevention of Achilles pain. Systematic reviews of insoles, footwear modification, and stretching found no clear benefit regarding prevention of lower extremity injuries in runners. B
Diagnosis is primarily clinical and based on precisely locating the patient's site of tenderness. B
Plain radiographs should be obtained initially for insertional Achilles pain to identify whether a fracture or Haglund's deformity is present. C
Since Achilles pain disorders have significant clinical overlap, ultrasound or MRI is useful in diagnosis and management. B

list.listitem: The diagnosis of Achilles pain disorders is primarily clinical.

Patients with Achilles tendinopathy typically complain of dull, aching pain which increases with activity. The pain typically limits activity. Physical exam reveals a tender swelling in the body of the Achilles tendon 3 to 4 cm above the calcaneal insertion.

Achilles enthesopathy also typically involves chronic and dull pain which increases with activity and limits exercise. The patient often has mild swelling and tenderness to palpation at the calcaneal insertion.

Retrocalcaneal or adventitial bursitis initially is sharp and stabbing. Erythema and swelling is commonly seen in the region of the Achilles insertion. In the case of adventitial bursitis, swelling and tenderness are located between the skin and the Achilles tendon. In retrocalcaneal bursitis, swelling and tenderness are most pronounced anterior and lateral to the Achilles tendon just above the insertion.
In all Achilles pain syndromes the athlete often describes a change in footwear or increased intensity of training that preceded their symptoms.
Haglund's deformity may be seen or palpated on physical exam, although formal diagnosis requires radiographs.
A positive Thompson test (absence of dorsiflexion of the foot with squeezing of the calf in the supine patient) is a reliable indicator of complete Achilles tendon rupture.
Different causes of Achilles pain often occur concurrently. Identifying the precise structure(s) responsible for Achilles pain is essential to determining the correct treatment strategy.
Haglund's deformity, which is associated with a worse prognosis with conservative therapy, is readily identified with plain radiographs.
Ultrasound and MRI can be used if a partial or complete Achilles tendon rupture is suspected. The choice imaging modality depends on local expertise.
No relevant clinical decision rules found.
See for the recommended approach to the patient.
Acute Achilles pain (symptoms less than 6 weeks in duration) is best treated with ice, stretching, and activity and footwear modification. C

Chronic Achilles tendinosis (more than 6 weeks in duration) should be treated with an eccentric exercise treatment program. Multiple studies show eccentric exercise to be effective for up to 90% of patients. A

NSAIDs should not be used to treat chronic Achilles tendinopathy or Achilles tendinopathy since they provide only modest alleviation of Achilles symptoms and do not address the underlying disease process. A
If 2 to 4 weeks of rest from the offending activity is not successful, Achilles enthesopathy should be treated with 4 to 6 weeks of immobilization with a walking boot. C
Eccentric exercises are less effective for Achilles enthesopathy. B
Changing footwear and relieving pressure are pivotal to treating retrocalcaneal and adventitial bursitis. C
Given the difficulty of proper placement and the potential risk for tendon rupture, corticosteroid injection of the Achilles tendon should be avoided in the primary care setting. C
NSAIDs, while commonly used to treat acute Achilles pain, provide only modest benefit in acute symptoms.
Surgical debridement may be indicated when patients fail to improve after prolonged conservative treatment or in patients with Haglund's deformity.
Before proceeding to surgery, patients with Achilles tendinopathy should have failed eccentric exercise and/or sclerosing injections since these conservative treatments have excellent response rates.

A randomized controlled trial of platelet rich plasma injection in 54 adult patients with chronic Achilles tendinopathy found no evidence of benefit compared with placebo injection. This negative result was confirmed in another RCT of 24 patients. Another RCT in 53 adult patients found no benefit of autologous blood injections.

A systematic review found no good evidence to support the effectiveness of glucocorticoid injections for Achilles tendinopathy. Evidence was limited, with only one randomized controlled trial identified.
Ice initially relieves pain and swelling.
Heel cups, U-Shaped heel pads and open backed shoes relieve the pressure that often exacerbates or causes Achilles enthesopathy, retrocalcaneal bursitis, or adventitial Achilles bursitis.

Eccentric exercises for tendinosis initially use body weight for resistance. The patient stands at the edge of a step with the ankle in the plantarflexed position then lowers to maximum dorsiflexion. The contralateral leg is used to return to the starting position.
The patient should do 3 sets of 15 with the knee flexed and with the knee extended twice a day for 10 to 12 weeks.
No additional exercise should be done for the first 6 weeks.
Patients should be warned that pain often increases during the first 10 to 14 days.
One study of 20 patients showed good outcomes at 4 years following loaded eccentric calf-muscle training for chronic Achilles tendinopathy.
Eccentric exercises can be employed for Achilles enthesopathy but are less effective. B

Ultrasound-guided sclerosing injections of neovessels is a promising new therapy for chronic Achilles tendinopathy. However, the longest cohort follow-up is only 2 years, where 38 of 42 patients were satisfied with sclerosing treatment after 24 months.
High energy extracorporeal shock wave therapy may be beneficial in treating Achilles enthesopathy.

In one RCT, combined eccentric loading training and shock-wave treatments were more effective for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy than training alone at 4 months, but differences were no longer present at 1 year.
In general, the evidence for using shockwave therapy in Achilles tendinopathy is conflicting and inconclusive.

A systematic review of 25 studies of low level laser therapy (LLLT) for tendinopathy found 12 positive trials and 13 negative or inconclusive trials. For achilles tendinopathy in particular, there was a mean 14 mm reduction in pain on a 100 mm scale (borderline clinical significance).
Refer to an orthopedist for multiple failures of prolonged conservative treatment of Achilles tendinosis.
Refer to an orthopedist within 24 hours for Achilles tendon rupture.
Refer to an orthopedist for failure of two trials of immobilization for insertional enthesopathy or of one trial of immobilization for insertional enthesopathy accompanied by Haglund's deformity.
Refer to a physical therapist if help is needed in teaching eccentric exercises.

Treatment course may be 12 weeks or longer for chronic Achilles tendinopathy or insertional Achilles enthesopathy. Monthly follow up allows for modification and progression of treatment strategies as needed. C
Achilles disorders accompanied by Haglund's deformity may still respond to conservative options, but typically have a prolonged course and often require surgical interventions. C
Isolated retrocalcaneal or adventitial bursitis responds well to changes in footwear usually within 4 weeks. C
Rest from activity and relief of pressure are critical to the treatment of insertional Achilles pain.

While doing eccentric rehabilitation for Achilles tendinosis, patients should abstain from running or other weight-bearing activities. Small case series of athletes who continue to train and perform while undergoing eccentric training show mixed results.
An increase in pain and discomfort is expected during the first 10 to 14 days of eccentric exercises.
